title: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
hook: a prince carries a water pot to a hut where two blind parents are waiting for their son
carry: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
tomorrow: Dasharatha's death and the curse, part three

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's death and the curse, part one. A young prince shot at a sound in the dark, and found a young ascetic with a water pot at the river. Did you catch yourself guessing before you looked? Day five hundred forty-three.

The young man in the river doesn't curse Dasharatha. That's the first surprise. He's dying, and what he talks about is his parents. They're old, he says, and both blind. They're sitting in a hut not far from here, thirsty, waiting for me to bring the water. Go to them. Tell them. And then he asks for one more thing: pull out the arrow. It's burning. The prince knows that if he pulls it, the boy will die. He does it anyway, because he was asked.
screen: `HE DOESN'T CURSE THE PRINCE.` → `MY PARENTS ARE BLIND AND THIRSTY.` → `PULL OUT THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: So Dasharatha fills the pot and walks the path the boy described. At the hut, the old father hears footsteps and speaks first. Why are you so late, son? Your mother was worried. Did we upset you? Say something. Picture the prince standing there with the water, hearing himself mistaken for the son he has just killed. And here is the moment the whole episode turns on. He could set the pot down and slip away. Nobody saw. Instead he tells them everything: who he is, the sound, the elephant he imagined, the arrow. In Valmiki's telling, the old father says something striking in reply. Because you told us yourself, he says, you are still alive. Had you hidden it, the consequences for you would have been far worse. The confession doesn't undo the death. But it changes what follows. The parents ask to be taken to their son. They sit with his body by the river, the mother and father touching his face, and they grieve aloud. The father then speaks the words that will shape the rest of Dasharatha's life. Just as I am losing my life in grief for my son, he says, you too will one day die grieving for a son. Then the old couple give up their lives on their son's funeral fire. Hold the strange double weight of this. The curse is terrible. And the old king tonight is telling Kausalya that it's coming true. Rama is gone. The son is lost to him. He knows exactly what's happening, because he was told, decades ago, by a father at a river.
screen: `WHY ARE YOU SO LATE, SON?` · `HE COULD SLIP AWAY. HE TELLS THEM.` · `YOU TOLD US YOURSELF.` · `YOU TOO WILL GRIEVE FOR A SON.` · then, large: `THE CURSE, COMING TRUE.`

segments.voice: Sit and let your breath slow down. Think of something small you once got wrong and never quite said out loud. Not the biggest thing. Something you can hold gently. Picture yourself telling it plainly to the person it touched, the way the prince told the old couple: what happened, nothing added, nothing hidden. You don't have to do anything about it today. Just notice how it feels to imagine saying it straight. The bell holds the time.
Dasharatha's death and the curse. The blind father's words: as I die grieving for my son, you too will die grieving for a son.
screen: `DASHARATHA'S DEATH AND THE CURSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it. Today, if you get something wrong, say so yourself before anyone has to find out. Day five hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: In many Hindu homes this episode is told as a story about duty to parents, and reciters dwell on the moment the prince tells the blind couple the truth instead of slipping away.

original.note: Sanskrit śāpa: a curse. in the epics, a curse spoken by an ascetic or a grieving parent is treated as certain to come true.

trapdoor: what you thought: the boy's family wants revenge.
what it means: the father's curse is grief speaking: you will lose a son as I have.
what a scholar hears: the father credits the confession with sparing the prince's life, a theme of admitted wrong that runs through the epics.

notes: Sarga numbers follow the vulgate numbering; confirm.
In Valmiki the boy also tells the prince he need not fear the sin of killing a Brahmin, giving his parents' birth. The script leaves this out; a Keeper may want it addressed.
The father's line about the confession sparing the prince (in some versions his head would have split) is paraphrased softly; confirm.
Some versions have the son appear in a heavenly form to his parents before they die; omitted here.
